results.title: Fireworks raises GPU rates up to 30% • The Weighted Average
results.author: Stephen Van Tran
highlights:
# Fireworks raises GPU rates up to 30%

09/01/26, 03:35 AM

 Follows up on Owning a Model Costs $124K per Benchmark Point 

Earlier analysis of Fireworks’ Training API argued that a narrow team should train its own model only when specialization pays back roughly $124,000 per benchmark point plus engineering cost. Fireworks’ current on-demand price table raises H100/H200 from $7 to $8 per GPU-hour, B200 from $10 to $13, B300 from $12 to $15, and GB300 from $18 to $20 starting September 1—an 11%–30% increase. The call holds: dedicated reinforcement training still belongs to a narrow buyer set, but new runs should use the higher rates because Fireworks prices reinforcement fine-tuning by GPU-hour.

results.title: DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it | Brown Forces Technology Studio
results.author: Salvador Alvarez
highlights:
# DigitalOcean jacks up GPU prices 20% — and you'll feel it

DigitalOcean just raised GPU instance prices by 20%, effective this week. The increase hits their A100 and H100 SKUs — the same chips every AI startup is fighting over. They're not the only one: Hetzner, OVH, and a handful of others have all lifted GPU rates over the past year. Supply for the good silicon is tight, and the big cloud providers have been pricing it like it's a luxury good ever since the LLM boom.

For a small shop running inference on a single A100, that's a real hit on the P&L. DigitalOcean's original pitch was cheap, predictable infrastructure for people who don't want to read a pricing spreadsheet — and this move breaks that promise. If you're training or serving models on DO, you'll want to check the new rates and compare against alternatives before committing to a long lease. The market is still hot; prices may move again.

results.title: Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI Push AI Rental Rates Higher as Delivery Tightens | Drip
highlights:
AI rental prices are climbing as cloud providers monetize the growing cost and scarcity of delivering usable GPU capacity.

Updated September 28, 2026

## What is this trend?

GPU rental rates are rising as cloud and AI operators pass through higher costs for power, cooling, and delivery constraints on already-contracted capacity.

- • Nebius, Oracle, and Vessl AI are raising prices on specific GPU offerings, not the whole market.
- • Scarcity is shifting from chips alone to deliverable capacity: power, cooling, and site readiness.
- • Utility delays and high-density racks are making retrofits and interconnects a billable constraint.
- • Operators with power and thermal control can command higher rents and better margins.
- • Pricing is fragmenting by region and SKU as guaranteed access becomes more valuable than headline supply.

## What’s the latest?

September 28, 2026

Nebius raised selected Nvidia GPU rates 17%–21%, Oracle renewed expiring GPU contracts about 20% higher, and Vessl AI lifted H100 pricing in Korea by 24.7%, where local H100 rentals were up 21.9% month over month to $3.2

Jared Carpenter

Product Update SaladCloud Tue Sep 01 2026

We're updating GPU and vCPU pricing on SaladCloud to correct places where our prices had drifted out of line with demand: some classes were priced above what the market will bear, and a couple were priced below it.

results.title: Neoclod GPU Prices Surge 25% in Q2, Data Center ROI Period Shrinks to 2 Years | Gate News
results.author: GateNews
highlights: According to Korea Investment & Securities analysts on August 1, neoclod companies reported significant GPU rental fee increases in Q2 results. CoreWeave implemented a 25% price increase across all products in July, while Nebius saw capacity auction prices 15% higher than previous highs. IREN's three-year contract rates jumped 125% versus November 2025, with five-year rates up 70%. results.title: NVIDIA B300 Pricing (September 2026) | Thunder Compute
results.author: Carl Peterson
highlights:
The NVIDIA B300 is one of the most powerful data center GPUs you can rent in 2026, built on the Blackwell Ultra architecture with 288 GB of memory per GPU. Demand is high and supply is still ramping, which keeps pricing volatile and access limited.

...

The practical question is what it costs to rent, and whether you need this much GPU at all.

This guide covers NVIDIA B300 cloud pricing for October 2026, including on-demand rates across providers. It also breaks down specs, compares the chip against the B200, H100, and H200, and shows which LLMs fit on a single card.

Takeaways

- B300 rates vary widely. On-demand rates start near $7.10/GPU-hr on neoclouds and reach $17.80 on hyperscalers.
- Its value is memory. 288 GB per card lets a single B300 hold very large models without sharding across multiple GPUs.
- Choose B300 only when you must. Very large model training or serving a model that overflows 180 GB.
- Thunder Compute roadmap. We don't offer B300 nodes. You can launch an H100 80GB at $3.20/hr, or 2x H100 for $6.40, with one-click VS Code, per-minute billing, and persistent storage.

...

## NVIDIA B300 Pricing

The B300 isn't sold as a standalone card, and NVIDIA doesn't publish list prices, so cloud rental is how the chip actually gets used. On-demand rates currently start near $7.10/GPU-hr on neoclouds and climb to $17.80 on hyperscalers.

results.title: The bill is increasing even though prices haven't been raised | What is actually happening with AWS, Azure, and GCP｜梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
results.author: 梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
highlights:
“AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud have not raised prices yet.”

This is a sentence that always comes up when talking about cloud costs since the beginning of 2026. And it is half true. As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that the three companies have collectively raised the base prices for general-purpose compute or storage.

The other half is the problem. GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice. In May, Google doubled certain network fees in North America. And all three companies officially have a mechanism for Japanese users where “the list price is in dollars, but the billing is in yen.” As long as this mechanism exists, even if the providers do not raise prices by a single cent, the billed amount will increase if the yen continues to weaken.

...

### There is certainly no sign of a blanket increase in base prices

I checked the AWS pricing page and What's New, Microsoft's licensing notices and Partner Center announcements, and the Google Cloud pricing change notification page. I went through them all, and as of September 2, 2026, there is no official announcement that base prices for general-purpose compute and storage are being raised across the board.

In response to an inquiry from DatacenterDynamics, AWS replied, “AWS's commitment to not raise pricing on fixed pricing models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged.” This is a statement that their policy of not raising prices for fixed-price models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged. The price revisions Microsoft made in 2026 were for Microsoft 365 (SaaS), which is a separate matter from the Azure infrastructure. What is listed on the Google Cloud “Infrastructure Services and Pricing Updates” page is still the content of the revisions implemented in October 2022 and April 2023.

...

### AWS GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice

However, it is not the case that there are no price increases at all.

AWS has a menu called EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allows you to reserve GPU computing resources for a set period. This pricing page states the following:

“Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks. The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in October, 2026.”

They are updated regularly based on supply and demand, with the next revision scheduled for October 2026. In other words, this menu is designed with the premise that prices will fluctuate.

In fact, it has moved twice since the beginning of 2026. In January, the p5e.48xlarge equipped with NVIDIA H200 was revised from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and the p5en.48xlarge was revised from $36.18 to $41.61. In July, after initially being announced for July 1 and then changed to July 7, the revisions covered P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The P6-B300 is at a level of $14.04 per hour per accelerator.

The prices for January mentioned here are only the amounts after the revision as of January. Because it went up again in July, the p5e.48xlarge currently on the pricing page is $47.76 per hour. That is exactly a 20 percent increase from $39.80.

AWS does not publish these revision rates. Since they do not keep old prices, the figures of “15 percent” and “20 percent” are calculated by news organizations and technical blogs that kept records of the price lists before and after the revisions. They are simply separate calculation results lined up, such as the January revision being exactly 15 percent and the July P5 revision being exactly 20 percent. It is not that AWS said “we are raising prices by 15 to 20 percent,” and the new and old prices themselves mentioned above are also based on the records of the reporting side.

And one more point. There are no individual notifications for these revisions in AWS's What's New or on their blog. What exists is the fact that the pricing page has been rewritten and the next scheduled update notice appearing in small print on that page. Price increases are being carried out in a way that you cannot notice unless you go looking for them.

### In May, Google doubled the transfer via peering in North America

Google Cloud also has one officially announced price increase for 2026.

The scope is egress transfer for CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering. The official Google page states, "Effective May 1, 2026, Google Cloud will implement pricing adjustments to the list prices for data transfer out through CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering," and the list prices have changed as follows.

- North America: $0.04 to $0.08 per 1GiB (2x)
- Europe: $0.05 to $0.08 (60 percent)
- Asia: $0.06 to $0.085 (approx. 42 percent)

Caution is required here. What was increased was transfer via peering, not Cloud CDN itself or general internet-bound egress transfer. Those pricing pages have no 2026 revision notice, and the egress notice page still shows the February 2024 implementation. If you generalize it as "Google raised network fees," the story becomes broader than the facts.

Note that Google does not provide a reason for this revision. The notice only contains the implementation date, the scope, and the old and new prices. This differs from how AWS explains Capacity Blocks based on supply and demand.

To summarize, the base prices of the three companies have not moved. What is moving are the quotas for AI computing resources and specific network paths.

### For all three companies, the list price is in dollars, but the billing is in yen.

This is where the main point begins. For users in Japan, there is actually a price hike that is having a more certain impact.

All three companies explain the same structure in their official documentation. The list price is set in US dollars, and billing is conducted in Japanese yen. The conversion rate is determined by each company using their own method.

...

The FAQ regarding Microsoft Customer Agreements specifically describes how the rate is determined.

"We use London closing spot rates that are captured in the two business days prior to the last business day of the previous month end. (Omitted) This rate applies to all transactions during the upcoming month."

The London closing spot rate captured two business days before the last business day of the previous month is applied to all transactions in the following month. The same page even provides an example where the rate for January is determined in the final days of December and applied to all Azure purchases and consumption in January. Since the rate is fixed within the month, the impact of the weak yen appears in monthly steps.

...

- As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud have generally raised base prices for general-purpose compute and storage.
- However, prices have risen in specific areas. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML were revised twice, in January and July 2026, and the pricing page states that the next revision is scheduled for October 2026. AWS has not disclosed the revision rate, and the "15 to 20 percent" figure circulating is a value back-calculated from the old and new prices.
- Google Cloud raised prices for egress via CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering starting May 1, 2026. In North America, the price doubled from $0.04 to $0.08 per GiB. Cloud CDN itself and general egress are not affected.
- For all three companies, the structure in Japan is that list prices are in dollars, while billing is in yen. Azure determines the rate based on the London closing price two business days before the end of the previous month, Google Cloud at the beginning of each month, and AWS at the time the invoice is created. The Japanese yen is not included in Google Cloud's currency fluctuation protection target currencies.
- Therefore, even if the provider does not raise prices, the billed amount will increase if the yen weakens. The standard foreign exchange rate has gone from 145 yen in July 2025 to 163 yen for the September 2026 application period.
- Domestically, Fujitsu will implement price revisions for FJcloud-V and others on October 1, 2026. The revision rates have not been publicly disclosed to that extent.
- In the State of FinOps 2026, 98 percent of organizations responded that they are managing AI spending (up from 31 percent two years ago), and SaaS spending management has reached 90 percent.

results.title: Nvidia Warns Hyperscalers of 15%+ Price Hikes on Rubin and Blackwell AI Systems
results.author: BabelWire AI Editor
highlights:
Nvidia's contract server builders have told Microsoft, Google, and Oracle that prices on AI server systems will rise more than 15% starting on shipments in early 2027, hitting flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell configurations.

Listen EN· AI synthesis·~1 min–:––

Nvidia's contract server builders have told Microsoft, Google, and Oracle that prices on AI server systems will rise more than 15% starting on shipments in early 2027, hitting flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell configurations.

The increase is driven by soaring DRAM costs from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron that Nvidia can no longer absorb even at its 75% gross margin. The pass-through is the first broad hyperscaler-facing sticker shock of the Rubin era.

This price increase could significantly impact AI infrastructure budgets for major cloud providers and may accelerate the development of alternative AI chip solutions as companies seek to reduce their dependence on Nvidia's increasingly expensive hardware.

results.title: packet.ai vs Nebius: GPU Cloud Comparison 2026 | packet.ai
highlights:
Nebius is a full-stack AI cloud with its own data centres and a rate card that starts at the H100. packet.ai starts at $0.39/hr. They overlap on exactly one card, and the gap on that card is 41%.

...

Nebius, the Amsterdam-headquartered AI infrastructure company spun out of Yandex, builds and operates its own data centres in Finland, France, the US and elsewhere, and sells GPU capacity from single VMs to InfiniBand clusters of thousands of GPUs. It has a full platform around the compute: managed Kubernetes, Slurm-based clusters, object storage, and a per-token inference service.

packet.ai is smaller and lower. It does not sell H100, H200 or B300 yet, and its cluster product is quoted rather than self-served. What it has is a B200 at 41% below Nebius's on-demand price and a set of workstation and Ampere cards Nebius does not list at all.

...

### What Nebius offers

Nebius's published on-demand rates in August 2026: HGX H100 $3.85/hr (preemptible $2.15), HGX H200 $4.50/hr (preemptible $2.45), HGX B200 $7.15/hr (preemptible $3.95), HGX B300 $7.85/hr (preemptible $4.30). Committed-use discounts run to 35%. Egress is free; standard object-storage egress is about $0.015/GiB. Earlier in 2026 the B200 was listed at $5.50/hr, so watch the trend.

- Own data centres in Finland, France, Iceland, the US and more; strong European data-residency story
- Managed Kubernetes, Slurm clusters, InfiniBand fabric, shared filesystem and object storage
- Preemptible tier at roughly 55% of on-demand across all cards
- No consumer or workstation GPUs; the rate card starts at the H100

...

Nebius's rate card starts at the H100. There is no A100, no L40S, no RTX 6000 Pro, no RTX 4090, nothing below datacentre-class Hopper and Blackwell silicon. If your workload fits an entry or mid-tier card, Nebius simply does not sell one. packet.ai's range runs from RTX 4090 at $0.39/hr up through B200, so most workloads that do not need an H100-class card land on a cheaper tier by default.

On the one card both platforms sell, B200, packet.ai is cheaper than Nebius on-demand. B200 starts at $4.25/hr Dynamic, non-interruptible, on packet.ai. Nebius's on-demand B200 is $7.15/hr, a 41% gap against packet.ai's Dynamic rate. Nebius's preemptible B200 is lower, at $3.95/hr, but can be reclaimed at any time.

...

Billing is hourly; the one monthly plan is 2× B200 Dedicated at $11,665.40/mo. There are no platform fees and no ingress charges; egress is $0.04/GB. Local storage is included with every instance, from 150 GB (RTX PRO 6000 Dynamic) to 2.8 TB (8× B200 Dedicated). Dynamic instances are SSH-ready in under five minutes, Dedicated in five to ten. Capacity is live in the US (California, Virginia, Texas, Oregon) and Europe (Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Paris, London, Dublin). H100 SXM, H200 and RTX 5090 are on the notify list.

...
